chapter_theme: Last songs at Kanchipuram (காஞ்சீபுரம், 3 of 3): the poet confesses infatuation with women and courtesans who take his wealth, the body's old age and death, and his own trade of praising unworthy patrons for money, and asks for the feet, a truth beyond the quarrelling sects, and a place among the devotees; the praise dwells on Uma's penance at Kanchi by the Kampa river, Krishna in the Bharata war, and Murugan as Siva's teacher.
structure_note: Songs on women and courtesans (338, 340, 342, 345, 346, 348, 349, 351); old age and death (341); songs of doctrine against the sects and toward the wordless truth (339, 343, 347, 350); a love-lament in another voice (344); and the poet's confession of praising patrons for gold (352). The Kanchi legend of Uma's penance and the Lord melting toward her recurs in 338, 350 and 352.

338.reading: Struck by Kama's flower arrows and taken by a woman whose kohl-dark, intoxicated eyes drew out his life, the poet asks to give up the experience of infatuation with her and be granted the lotus feet that are the substance of the house of supreme bliss taught in Vedanta. The praise names Siva Ekambara clothed in the directions, and Uma who joined him at Kanchi of the dharmas, and Murugan who embraced the huntress, let Indra's city live, and drew the vel that dried the sea and uprooted the night-walkers.
338.nuance: வேதாந்த பரமசுக வீடாம் பொருள் இதவிய பாதாம்புயம்: the feet are themselves the Vedantic goal, the bliss of release, set against the அநுபோகம் of the woman. ஏகாம்பர names Siva of the Kanchi temple. The epithets of Siva in lines 12 to 14 (அமகர, அதுலன நீலாம்பரம் அறியாத, அநகர நாளாங்கிதர்) are hard to divide.

339.reading: The poet sets aside the quarrelsome, ill-natured followers of the sects, who find no single way to end karma-born birth and stagger among the doubts and contradictions of their many texts, and asks Murugan to tell him, so that he does not perish, the true form filled with silence that the mind cannot reach. The praise is of Krishna, refuge of the five Pandavas, who drove the chariot through the eighteen days on the field of the Kurus until the kshatriyas died, and calls Murugan his nephew at Kachi.
339.nuance: கலக காரண துற்குண சமயிகள்: the sects are not merely wrong but causes of quarrel, and their many-class texts breed விகற்பம் and விபரீதம். Against them the goal is மவுன பூரித சத்திய வடிவு, a truth filled with silence. நாளோர் பத்தெட்டு, eighteen days, and தேர்கடவு அச்சுதன, Achyuta driving the chariot, name the Kurukshetra war, told at unusual length for a praise section.

340.reading: After a long picture of women with ringing anklets, gem-hung breasts, rolling sword-eyes, pearl smiles and cloud-dark hair who speak flirtatious words, the poet asks whether kinship with them is fitting. The praise is mostly of Uma, the golden lady who kept her grace on him and ruled him, Parvati joined in Siva's form, Sivakami, the dancer who saw the three worlds, Sambhavi, and of Murugan her son, whose vel burned the asura clans and who loves Devayanai and the wise huntress, at Kanchi.
340.nuance: எனையருள் வைத்திட்டு ஆண்ட நாயகி: the poet claims the goddess's grace on himself, not only on Murugan. The many names of Uma (சிவை, சுடர், சத்தி, சாம்பவி, அமை) make the praise a hymn to the Shakti of Kanchi, as in 32. The plea itself is only a rhetorical question; தூவையர் is unclear.

341.reading: The poet pictures old age and death: teeth fall like clusters, the ruined coat of the body stops working, the man turns white as a crane, bent over a stick, yawning, his breath going out, and then the kin cry 'he is dead, I am ruined, ah, oo', burn him, leave and go; he asks whether that bewilderment will not end. The praise calls Murugan the eternal Kumaresa of Kachi who stands for the peacock, who fought Sura in the long sea, and the unending, pure, released lord of release.
341.nuance: The song is set in hard, clipped syllables, and the kin's wailing is given as sound (அஆ உஉ). குப்பாயம், a coat, is the body worn and thrown off. The last line runs epithets of release (முற்றா நித்தா அத்தா சுத்தா முத்தா முத்தி). The close of the plea (அப்பேதுத்துக்கு அமறாதோ) is unclear in division.

342.reading: A short song: the poet asks not to wander clinging to what suits sin, the women with coral lips and bodice-bound breasts, but to be given a heart of devotion so that he may sing. The praise names the vel that pierced the mango tree, Murugan sweet to the parrot of the ruby heaven, with the cock in his golden hand, lord of Kachi and emperor of the gods' heaven.
342.nuance: பாடப் பத்திச் சித்தம்: devotion is asked for as the condition of song. The mango (மா) is Sura in his tree form.

343.reading: The poet seems to rebuke himself ('fie!') for having tasted jivanmukti and experience, burning the three cities to ash and uprooting the sheath of sleep, and yet, not knowing how to stay settled in grace, having run off and let go; he asks Murugan to hold him so he does not end on the ruined road and to grant the lotus feet. The praise names Siva with trident, deer and axe and Uma at his side, whose golden guru Murugan is, and lists the shrines where Murugan receives worship three times a day: Kasi, Madurai, the seven hills, Kovalur, Vedaranyam, Kazhi, Arur, Puliyur, Kalatti, Chiramalai and Kanchi.
343.nuance: சீவன் முத்தியிற் கூடவே களித்து அநுபூதி சேர: the plea speaks of liberation in life and அநுபூதி, the direct experience of the Lord, as something reached and then lost. The three cities (முப்புரம்) and the sheath of sleep (நித்திரைக் கோசம்) seem to be inner, not mythic. The list of shrines in the praise is a small map of Tamil and northern holy places.

344.reading: In the voice of one who watches over a lovesick girl, the singer asks that this child, who came to desire without yet knowing desire, not waste away under the stained moon the serpent seeks and the sea roaring with its conches and waves, and that Murugan come and say 'do not fear'. The praise names him with the green peacock, the green hunter maid and the green hills, the one whose anklets his devotees serve, the Kachi lord of the shining vel who freed the bound hands of the gods of the kalpaka grove.
344.nuance: The whole song is built on doubled words with different senses (நச்சரவம், பச்சை, பத்தி, கச்சி, கற்பக): a யமகம். இச்சையுணர்வின்றி இச்சையென வந்த இச்சிறுமி: the girl is too young to know what she feels. This is akam, not the poet's confession.

345.reading: The poet confesses that with deceitful conduct and a foolish heart he gave much real wealth to the quick-talking jesting women to please them until his life withered, and now lives in poverty that burns like the undersea fire; he asks that, his cunning gone, hell left behind and the two deeds cut, he be given the feet. The praise names Murugan who embraced the huntress at Kachi, his chest hung with kuravu, vetchi, lotus and kuvalai flowers, guru to Siva who burned the cities with his long bow, and the one who crushed the nirudas' army by the sea.
345.nuance: மிடியெனப் பெரு வடவை சுட்டிய விதனம்: poverty is the வடவை fire under the sea, the result of what he gave the women, so the courtesan's charge is told from its end. மெய்ப்பொருள் may be wealth or 'true substance', a pun on what he threw away.

346.reading: The poet describes ornamented women with cuckoo voices who speak Kama's words and jesting talk, then talk money and send go-betweens, impure of heart, greedy for many men's leavings, and asks whether such company befits him. The praise, after a drum passage of battle, names Kandavel who angrily struck on the head the Veda-learned god of the lotus, child of the one with the discus, and who married the guardian of the millet field, at Kanchi.
346.nuance: பணமெத்தப் பேசித் தூதிடும் ... பலர் எச்சிற்கு ஆசைக் காரிகள்: money and many men, the two stock charges. The praise alludes to the punishment of Brahma (மறைகற்ற புத்தேள், the lotus-dweller born of Vishnu) but does not say here that it was for not knowing Om.

347.reading: The poet asks for That which is hard to tell people, cannot be reached by learning, has no likeness, cannot be measured by the mind or caught in the chain of tattvas, which was the meaning taught to the three-eyed Siva, the cause of release, out of fools' reach, and which the four Vedas say they cannot reach even at their height. The praise names the vel that pierced the great Sura's chest, Vishnu's admiration, and Murugan who played before the mother whose chastity holds although she bore all seven worlds, at the Kachchalai of Kachi.
347.nuance: The plea is built of negations (முடியாதது, ஒவாதது, படாதது, எட்டாதது): a way of speaking of the Absolute rather than the poet's own state. முக்கண் ... அருசாவிய அர்த்தக்குப் போதகம்: the meaning Siva asked to hear is the teaching of Siva, without Om named. கற்பு தப்பாது உலகேழையும் ஒக்கப் பெற்றாள்: the virgin mother of all worlds. One word in the praise (வெருபம்) may be garbled.

348.reading: The poet asks whether he, Murugan's servant, should swoon, his mind destroyed and wasted, by a woman's dull infatuation, her deceitful words, deer and spear eyes, moon forehead, swan gait and bangled hands. The praise names Kumaresa who once circled the world on the peacock in an instant, the Murugesa given by the mountain daughter who shares Siva's side, at Kampai city of tall jewelled mansions.
348.nuance: அறிவே அழிந்து அயர்வாகி நைந்து: the harm named is to understanding, not to wealth. The circling of the world is the contest for the fruit; கம்பை is Kanchi by the Kampa river.

349.reading: The poet lists the courtesans, priced women decked in pearl and gem strings, sinful, tricky, cheating, with leaf-like sword eyes and smiles, whose way of life brings sickness of mind and sores, and asks whether he must wander on that path. The praise, after drum syllables, names the vel that sank the enemies and their mountain of sorrow in the red sea, Murugan as guru to Siva the dancer smeared with ash, and the husband of the girl of the hill village, at Kachi.
349.nuance: விலைமாதர், women with a price, is named outright, and சித்த நோய்ப் புண் joins the mind's sickness to the body's sores. கற்புரத்தை வீட்டி is unclear: perhaps Siva destroying the stone (or triple) cities.

350.reading: The poet praises those who leave behind the mischievous, wave-loud sects and their hard mass of learning, who with minds free of attachment, by grace, without distraction, know Murugan, melt and reach his golden lotus feet, and asks whether he will not think of placing him too with love in their company. The praise names the twelve-armed hero whose vel broke a mountain and Sura, and Murugan of Kachi by the Kampa river, where the Mother did penance so that her chastity toward Siva's arms would not fail.
350.nuance: தங்குழாத்தினில் என்னையும் வைக்க: the request is not for release directly but for a place in the gathering of devotees. கம்பையாற்றினில் அன்னை தவம்புரி: the Kanchi legend of Uma's penance by the Kampa river is named. கன்னமிடும் (housebreaking) in the first line may charge the sects with robbing minds; the division is uncertain.

351.reading: After describing women's carp-like eyes that dart, rival arrows and reach the ears, the poet says that even if he falls at their feet and goes on in this way, he will not forget the one word. The praise, through drum syllables, names Murugan as guru to the dancing Siva at the time of the great flood, the great one, and the lord of famed Kanchi who sang in Tamil that the bond is like magnet and needle.
351.nuance: ஓர் மொழி மறவேனே: the plea is turned into a vow; the one word may be the Lord's name or a mantra. காந்தக் கல்லும் ஊசியுமே என ஆய்ந்து தமிழ் ஓதிய: the magnet and the needle is the Saiva image of the Lord drawing the soul. The flood (பெருநீர் வெள்ளம்) may be the Kampa flood of the Kanchi legend. Several lines of the praise are hard to divide.

352.reading: The poet confesses that he made poems praising senseless, ungrateful, deceitful men who never bow to Murugan's feet, wandered blessing them in search of wealth, gathered a little, and poured it out on women while roaming the streets; he asks that this disgrace be removed and that release be given clearly. The praise tells how Uma came on the bull to Kachi to do penance and remove her darkness and the Lord melted toward her, and how Murugan, whose words Siva hears, entered among the hunters as an old man and embraced the girl who chased the birds, at Kumarakottam.
352.nuance: The confession is of the poet's own trade: praising unworthy patrons (அவலர் மேல் சொற்கள் கொண்டு கவிகள் ஆக்கி) and spending the gain on women. இருளை நீக்கத் தவஞ்செய்து அருள நோக்கிக் குழைந்த: the Kanchi legend of Uma's penance and Siva's melting toward her. குமரகோட்டம் is the Murugan shrine at Kanchi.

links.note: Both picture old age by teeth lost and a body bent on a stick. The Naladiyar uses it against the old man who still desires; 341 carries the picture on to the corpse burned and the kin going home.

Both are laments in another voice for a girl lovesick for Murugan, worn down by the night's sights and sounds: in 24 the crescent, the south wind and the anril bird, in 344 the stained moon and the roaring sea.
The Kural warns that women who desire a man for his wealth bring him harm; 345 tells the harm from inside, the wealth given away and a poverty that burns like the undersea fire.

source_issues: Song 343: one corrupt character in புலி஧வ்ளுர் (line 21), probably புலியூர் (Chidambaram).
Song 351: one corrupt character in லு஡ர்ந்து (line 3), probably ஊர்ந்து.
Song 349: heading variant '( காஞ்சீபுரம் )' recorded by the source.
